content.overview: Technician I workers must recognize common cultivation hazards, judge whether an authorized routine control is sufficient, and stop or escalate work when the condition is unsafe, prohibited, changing, or outside their authority.

vocabulary.definition: A source or condition with the potential to cause injury, illness, damage, or loss.
The combination of the likelihood of harm and the severity of the possible consequence.
A prevention framework that prioritizes removing or reducing hazards at the source before relying only on procedures or personal protective equipment.
A deliberate pause in work when conditions are unsafe, prohibited, uncontrolled, or outside the worker's authority.

sections.title: Recognize the real work environment
sections.body: NIOSH identifies chemical, biological, ergonomic, physical, electrical, fire, cut, slip, trip, fall, heat, noise, ultraviolet-light and other hazards in cannabis work. A technician should deliberately scan people, pathways, equipment, materials, environmental conditions and alarms instead of normalizing a hazard because it is familiar.

sections.title: Prefer stronger controls, but stay inside your role
sections.body: Effective prevention favors eliminating or reducing the hazard at its source before relying only on reminders or PPE. Technician I workers apply the strongest control they are trained and authorized to perform, verify that it worked, and escalate engineering, electrical, mechanical, life-safety or other technical changes that require qualified personnel.

sections.title: Risk changes while work is happening
sections.body: A task that began normally can become unsafe when water spreads, a guard is missing, an alarm activates, a route becomes blocked, a chemical cannot be identified, or equipment begins behaving abnormally. The technician reassesses the condition rather than treating the original work order as permission to continue under changed conditions.

workedExamples: A hose crossing a main aisle is placed on the approved hanger and the path is rechecked before work continues.
Visible electrical damage near a wet area is taken out of use and escalated rather than investigated live by an unqualified worker.
A cart blocking a marked route is moved using the normal material-handling procedure and the route is verified clear.
A machine guard is missing before startup, so the equipment is not used and the out-of-service or escalation procedure is followed.
commonMistakes: Treating a familiar hazard as acceptable because no injury has occurred yet.
Choosing a weak reminder or warning when an authorized physical correction is available.
Attempting a repair, bypass or technical adjustment outside training or authorization.
Assuming a scheduled task must continue even after conditions change.
content.practicalApplication: Inspect a mock cultivation work area, identify at least six hazards or abnormal conditions, rank the first response as routine control, stop/isolate, escalation or emergency response, and justify the decision using the observed condition and the worker's authority boundary.
content.summary: Safe cultivation work requires deliberate hazard recognition, preference for stronger controls, reassessment when conditions change, and clear authority boundaries. Correct stop-work and escalation are part of competent performance.

blocks.title: Start with observation, not normalization
blocks.body: A wet aisle, damaged cord, unstable ladder, blocked walkway, sharp tool, leaking line, unguarded moving part, chemical splash risk, hot work area or unsafe gas condition should not become invisible simply because workers see it every day. Recognition comes before production pressure.

blocks.alt: Simplified cultivation room showing irrigation water approaching damaged electrical equipment, a blocked aisle, an unstable ladder, an exposed cutting tool, high-intensity lighting, and a carbon-dioxide life-safety alarm, with a reminder to scan for other task-specific exposures.
blocks.caption: Use a deliberate room scan: people, pathways, equipment, environment, materials and alarms.

blocks.title: Five questions for a pre-task and mid-task hazard scan

items.title: People
items.body: What can injure, expose, strain, trap or distract a worker during this task?

items.title: Pathways and access
items.body: Are aisles, exits, ladders, platforms, carts, hoses and work surfaces in a controlled condition?

items.title: Equipment and environment
items.body: Is any guard, cord, alarm, line, controller, light, gas monitor or environmental condition outside its expected state?

items.title: Materials and identity
items.body: Can every chemical, tool and material required for the task be positively identified and used under the current procedure?

items.title: Authority
items.body: Is the needed response within your training, assigned procedure and authorization? If not, who owns the next decision?

blocks.title: Control strength and Technician I decision boundaries
rows: Remove or physically correct the hazard
Place a hose on the approved hanger so it no longer crosses the aisle
Use the routine approved control, then verify the hazard is actually removed
Guarding, ventilation, interlock, electrical repair or equipment modification
Recognize failure or need; do not modify technical safeguards unless specifically trained and authorized
Restricted route, housekeeping rule, task sequence, signage or controlled procedure
Follow the current instruction and report when the control is missing, unclear or ineffective
Task-specific protection selected for the assessed exposure
Use the required PPE correctly; do not treat PPE as permission to ignore an uncontrolled hazard

blocks.title: Recognition is not repair authority
blocks.body: Recognizing a damaged electrical device, unsafe alarm condition, failed guard or technical fault does not automatically authorize a Technician I worker to open, repair, bypass or troubleshoot it. Stop or isolate where the site procedure authorizes that action, preserve the condition, and escalate.

blocks.alt: Flowchart showing a technician observing a hazard, checking for an authorized routine control, applying and verifying that control when permitted, or stopping, isolating where authorized, and escalating when the task cannot proceed safely. Life-safety alarms direct the worker to the posted emergency procedure.
blocks.caption: A practical decision model for routine controls, stop-work, isolation within authorization, escalation and emergency response.

blocks.title: Routine control versus unauthorized technical repair

left.label: Routine control
left.body: A hose partly blocks an aisle and the approved hanger is available. Place the hose on the hanger, verify the path is clear, and continue according to procedure.

right.label: Technical fault
right.body: A powered device has visible cord damage near water. Do not open or test the wiring. Stop use, prevent exposure where authorized, and escalate to the qualified person or team.

blocks.title: Water approaching damaged electrical equipment
blocks.setting: You enter a corridor and see irrigation water spreading toward a powered device with visible cord damage. The task list says irrigation must begin immediately.
blocks.prompt: What should control the next action?
options: Continue because the task is scheduled
Dry only the visible water and keep using the device
Stop the task, prevent exposure where authorized, and escalate the electrical condition
Open the device to see whether the wire is actually energized
blocks.answer: Stop the task, prevent exposure where authorized, and escalate the electrical condition.
blocks.feedback: Production timing does not override an uncontrolled electrical hazard. Technician I should not perform unauthorized electrical investigation or repair.

blocks.title: The task changed after startup
blocks.setting: A routine material-movement task begins with a clear aisle. Ten minutes later a leak creates a spreading wet area and a cart now blocks part of the designated route. The work order itself has not changed.
options: Finish the move because the original work order was valid
Reassess the changed conditions, apply authorized routine controls if sufficient, and stop or escalate anything that remains uncontrolled
Walk around the condition without documenting it
Wait for the next shift because only supervisors can notice hazards
blocks.answer: Reassess the changed conditions, apply authorized routine controls if sufficient, and stop or escalate anything that remains uncontrolled.
blocks.feedback: Authorization to perform a task does not freeze the risk assessment. Technicians must respond to meaningful changes in the work environment.

blocks.title: Classify, justify and verify the first response
blocks.instructions: For each condition, classify the first response as routine control, stop/isolate, escalation or emergency response. State the observation that drove the classification, the control you are authorized to use, and how you would verify the condition is controlled before continuing.
prompts: A hose partly blocks an aisle and can be placed on the approved hanger.
A ladder has a damaged step.
An unknown life-safety alarm is sounding in an enriched room.
A small spill is fully covered by the site's routine spill procedure.
A powered hand tool has a damaged cord.
A cart blocks a marked emergency route.
A machine guard is missing before startup.
The task conditions change after work begins.
blocks.artifact: Hazard-response worksheet with classification, authority boundary, verification and escalation fields

blocks.title: Remediation cue
blocks.body: If your answer depends on 'being careful,' 'working faster,' 'using extra PPE,' or 'finishing because the task is scheduled,' reconsider the control. Competent performance asks whether the hazard is actually controlled and whether the proposed action is inside your authorization.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Safe routine cultivation work depends on noticing hazards early, preferring stronger authorized controls, verifying that the control worked, reassessing changed conditions, and treating stop-work and escalation as competent performance—not as failure to finish the task.
